commentBody: For me, kind of fast today. Had trouble with "Truth alternative".

OK, let's get this out of the way from the start.

28D changed its name from NAURU to Naoero last week.  It was in all the news reports.

That is all.

Great to see some Hip-Hop legends in WU-TANG CLAN and Dr. DRE included in today's puzzle. August 11, 1973 - DJ Kool Herc's Back to School party in the South Bronx is widely recognised as the official start of Hip-Hop culture. Happy 53rd Birthday!
Nice clues. I enjoyed it.
DOI slowed me down. Love WUTANGCLAN.

I'm still not sure when to write "disc "and when "disk." But obviously it was "chide" and not "khide," so I was able to correct. Other than that, a quick Tuesday.  It was nice not to have too much crosswordese.
NAURU is no longer its name! A few months ago it officially changed to “Naoero”. I bet the change happened after this puzzle was written!
Watch out on 28 down, editors! NYT just reported on a name change! 🤣 https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/03/world/naoero-nauru-name-change.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share

Love, love that this puzzle has more modern references. I would much rather see those than something like OLEO.

(And I do realize that WU-TANG CLAN was formed in 1992. It's still more modern than OLEO.)

Congratulations on a very good debut. Looking over the list of dynasties, it's hard to find other examples that work. Possibly [What might come out of the closet] -- CLOTHE(S HANG)ER. The SHANG dynasty is China's first verifiable dynasty, lasting approximately 550 years. But others? Pretty hard. I dare someone to find a good one for QING, the last dynasty, which ended in 1912. Some other ones equally hard: XIA, QIN (easy enough, but a commonly used phrase?), YUAN, ZHOU. SUI might be too easy, but suit yourself. 

Must proudly admit to watching with rapt attention "Dynasty" on TV starting with the second season, probably 1983, when Joan Collins, the Machiavellian beauty, schemed her way into my post-adolescent heart. I liked Dynasty much better than Dallas, its rival, chiefly because of Dame Joan's devotion to her role. Can't say I've ever read anything of hers, my low-brow inclinations have a limit, but she was a dynasty unto herself, in her time. 

Funny, I guessed ADVIL as popular tablets, a bit tired of IMacs and IPads, but that's on me. Also paused a time because I'm more likely to say, suspiciously, You're UP TO something and not the more positive, ON TO . Likewise, I'm more prone to saying I'll ADMIT it than I'll ALLOW it. Puzzles allow us to psychoanalyze ourselves.

A very clever and unique theme. I love that the constructor even threw in a Chinese DUMPLING.

As it happens I listen to HANS ZIMMER every night. He’s the composer of the ABC World News Tonight theme. 

Congratulations, Wade. A fine debut!
"an ewe"?
Someone's got to say it... This puzzle is for the children!

This was my best Tuesday time ever and yesterday was my best Monday. What a rush! Excited for Wednesday.

P.S. Loved the NIALL Horan reference, what a throwback.
Great debut, congrats!
Crosswords Rule Everything Around Me

Welcome aboard, Mr. Bednar, and congratulations on your debut! The SONG going through my head as I solved was "Don't know much about (Chinese) history..." so I'm glad this was a breezy Tuesday puzzle and all was gettable. Very happy to see HANS ZIMMER get a shout-out. Brilliant composer. So he's finally made it into the NYT crosswords? I'm sure his Oscars and Grammys will pale by comparison. *Now* he's arrived! :-) Here he is in Prague, playing "Time" (with, yes, Johnny Marr of The Smiths on guitar!) – https://youtu.be/va1oiojnGrA?is=9vD53a2AvS-xv3za Mario, Wario, LUIGI...everything I know about Mario Brothers I learned from the NYT xwords. As for NAURU, I thought it was funny that it showed up today. Just last week I noted here that I was trying to commit the new name to memory, thinking the abundance of vowels would land Naoero in a puzzle. I feel bad for the editors that an addendum to the clue fell through the cracks. Maybe it will show up tomorrow? Thank you, Mr. Bednar for a very nice puzzle. We'll done!

Wade, congrats on your debut! It’s always a pleasure to see a construction that reflects its constructor’s passions and apparently this includes two of yours—thanks for sharing!

Very tight theme considering the constraint of musicians/composers and the limitations of the dynasty name—quite remarkable, actually. I expect there will be some push-back in the comments about the number of proper nouns (even apart from the theme), which is a fair critique: I hope they will be kind; if not remember everyone has their own opinion and expectations. Don’t let it dampen your achievement!

I enjoyed it immensely and was able to get all the proper nouns that I didn’t know from crosses.

Anyone else try DIAN Fossey before NOAH? Great clue, that! How about RUBBER before RUBIES?

Also surprised that editors didn’t change the clue for NAURU. I expect the former name will stay around for a while but deserves to be recognized as such. After all, SIAM finally got the update!

Congratulations again, Wade, hope to see more of you!

I fully understand why “NAURU” was included, as the puzzle was surely constructed before the recent name change to “Naoero.” However, I’m very surprised a comment wasn’t included in the notes. 
Of all the times to add a little wisdom, this detail is just begging for elaboration.
Nice debut!  Fun puzzle with some thinky clues.  Embarrassingly I didn't fully realize the theme until reading the column after solving.  Very impressive.

Wade you made my Tuesday evening a blast! You have quite an eclectic taste in music. I hope to see more of your puzzles. I was sure 56A was doi as in duh, of course. Do I makes more sense, but I would be more inclined to answer doi.

The Wordplay column says [54D. Oh, the many four-letter places [What icicles do] could go! My first guess was “hang,” and my second was “drop.” I was one letter off from the correct answer, DRIP.]

I thought of MELT.

I went down the rabbit hole to find out that 59A [Big export of Myanmar] RUBIES are the most prized in the world but are also boycotted because of political issues there. From a NYT article called "Burmese Rubies: Costly and Controversial" https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/22/fashion/jewelry-rubies-myanmar-mozambique.html "Second only to colored diamonds in value, fine unheated Burmese rubies command exceptional prices per carat at major auction houses." "Due to political conflict, strict import regulations, and past embargoes, many international jewelers require extensive documentation or turn to alternative origins like Mozambique."
How do you get down from an elephant?  You don't - you get down from a duck.

The NAURU/ Naoero controversy is unfortunate, but not terribly surprising given how recently the name change happened. I assume the puzzle was given the green light months ago, and  there’s no staff dedicated to revisiting puzzles and looking for clues that have changed in the brief interim.

I suggest we give the clue editors a little grace. And I suspect most of us got there anyway, so what’s the problem, really?
Today I Learned - Don't do the crossword puzzle when you keep falling asleep.  I hit Check Puzzle when trying to do something else.  Darn.   That's it.  Off to bed.
I'd like to apologize to the good people of Myanmar for believing — for far too long — that they were big exporters of RABIES. Sorry!

An excellent puzzle that managed to have both easy gimme zones (the NE corner!) and some areas stuffed with real ticklish stumpers. 

I tried the “Across clues only” challenge and my bumpy progress eventually foundered on SYSCO and AOKAY, and it turned out i had rubber instead of RUBIES. I’m proud to say i got all three band names by puzzling them out. 

I clung to the “Ming” DYNASTY for too long, but eventually relented, with some surprise that the answer was SONG. Today i learned!

The Battle of Hastings was fought between two armies of about 7000 men each in 1066. It is one of the most important battles in history and known to every Briton (and maybe many more across the world.) At the same time the SONG DYNASTY had more than 1,000,000 soldiers. It was fighting the Mongols with rocket-propelled arrows, flamethrowers, crossbow snipers who could assassinate enemy generals, and fleets of warships. It’s no wonder that the Mongols, who eventually beat the Song, found conquering Europe such a cakewalk. More here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_history_of_the_Song_dynasty
Crazy clues for a Tuesday. Will, get it together.

Also loved the mini themette with ELM/ELMO OUT/OUTER.
Yes, the Island nation has changed its name to better represent the native tongue, but I think we can forgive the team for not picking up on it. I’m sure the choice and print date is decided so far in advance it’s difficult to flyspeck every one right before publishing.

"What kind of down is that? Goose?"
"No, EIDER."

This is a tight theme (Hi, @SP!).  I’m guessing that there aren’t going to many theme answer possibilities (with dynasties not used in today's grid) showing up in the comments today.  

But the Crosslandia gods smiled on Wade, because the theme answers he did find broke into two pairs with equal letter counts, to enable grid symmetry.  I would like to have seen the fist pump he made when he discovered that!

But first a constructor has to come up with the theme itself – and the idea for today’s theme – musical entities that contain Chinese dynasties – IMO, was a stroke of brilliance.  So quirky!  Never been done before, I’m sure.

That comes from a mind I'd like to see more puzzles from.

Bravo on all this and on your NYT debut, Wade, and there were enough no-knows for me (fairly crossed) to give my brain the work it cherishes.  I loved this puzzle from start to finish.  Thank you!

Didn’t care much for this one. A fine effort but I feel editorial really should’ve worked with the constructor to make something that really shines. It was a rather dull debut and it felt like it. 

A lot of the answers felt like the constructor was simply replacing more commonly understood meanings or definitions of words for second definitions or slight variations — baa/MAA, VIA rather than ala, SORES, MERE, AURA — or else making it trivia fest. 

I appreciate some fresh answers like FLAMINGLIPS and WUTANGCLAN, but this puzzle felt bumpy and uneven, like the constructor didn’t have a confident hold on it. 

Again, this is mostly on editorial. I think they really failed here.

Still don’t understand the complaints. Isn’t the idea of a puzzle to figure out the answers? Just filling in the answers that one already knew would be more like an exam. We all approach it with a different perspective and life experience. This creator is a recent college graduate; I graduated over fifty years ago.  Solving a puzzle bridges an age gap. Clever descriptions and clues to help figure it out is the fun part and then you have the increased knowledge for the future !

Not too long ago I saw someone post about how that person and a partner made a game out of how they solved Wordle I believe. I love how we puzzlers make puzzles out of the puzzles. I am a boomer and my zoomer niece and I have our own twist to puzzle solving. We each solve(or not)  strands, connections, the midi and spelling bee. Her fifth puzzle is Wordle, minus the crossword. We text each other our results. Our scoring system is: three solved= top hat emoji for her, straw hat for me; (I don't know how to add emojis here) four solved= trophy emoji (four=EGOT, hence the trophy); five solved= a diamond ring (ring for the five Olympic circles) Happy puzzling and have a good day!
